name: Camera language
controls: Whether the viewer's point of view moves through the graphic world, and how: framing, lens, angle, and the moves (pans, dollies, orbits, zooms, focus shifts) that change what the viewer sees without the objects themselves moving.
question: Should the frame stay still while things move, or should the camera travel through the world?
notes: Two different ways of making a frame change. Moving objects in a static frame: the frame is a fixed window, like a stage; elements enter, exit, transform and rearrange inside it; composition is authored per state. Moving the camera through the graphic world: the elements are laid out in a larger (often spatial) world, and the viewer's point of view travels across or into it; everything shifts together, coherently, because the viewer moved, not the objects. Camera language makes graphics feel cinematic and spatial and creates continuity across scenes; static framing reads as clearer, more graphic and more UI-like. Most pieces mix both: objects animate inside the world while a slow camera drifts. In a HyperFrames build, put all world content inside a single camera wrapper (e.g. #world) and animate only that wrapper for camera moves (translate for pan/track, scale for zoom, rotate for roll, perspective container plus translateZ for dolly); objects animate independently inside it. Set transform-origin on the wrapper to the point of interest before scaling, or compensate with translation. Key distinctions: a dolly moves the camera toward the subject, so perspective changes and near layers grow faster than far ones (parallax), while a zoom changes focal length, magnifying everything uniformly with no parallax; in 2D, scaling the whole world container is a zoom, and a dolly must be faked by scaling depth layers with different multipliers or by translateZ inside a perspective container. A pan rotates the camera on the spot (in reality almost no parallax), while a track (also called truck) moves the camera sideways, producing parallax; in flat 2D both collapse to a translate, so differentiate with layer multipliers. Terminology varies: in the US 'tracking shot' usually means a lateral move, while in the UK 'track in' often means a dolly in; 'push-in' is widely used for a slow dolly in. Framing terms (wide, macro, extreme close-up) and projection terms (top-down, orthographic, isometric) describe the camera's placement and lens rather than a move; they can be combined with any move.

options.what: The frame never moves; all change happens through objects moving inside a fixed window.
options.looks: A stable composition in which elements enter, transform and exit; margins and grid stay fixed.
options.motion: All motion belongs to objects: slides, scales, morphs, reveals. The frame is a stage.
options.use: UI demos, kinetic typography, data visualization, Swiss and minimalist motion, explainers.
options.vs: A slow drift is a camera move, even if subtle. Scaling one object is object motion; scaling the whole world is a camera zoom.
options.prompt: Keep the camera locked: no world-container transforms at any point. All change happens through elements entering, exiting, transforming and rearranging inside the fixed frame, respecting constant margins and grid.

options.what: The camera rotates horizontally on the spot, sweeping the view left or right.
options.looks: The view slides sideways across a wide scene; with a real camera, near and far elements barely shift relative to each other.
options.motion: Smooth horizontal sweeps with ease-in-out; in 3D, slight perspective skew at the frame edges.
options.use: Revealing wide scenes, following a subject sideways, scanning a timeline or a row of features.
options.vs: A track (truck) moves the camera sideways and creates parallax; a pan rotates it on the spot with minimal parallax. Whip pan is a pan so fast it blurs.
options.prompt: Pan by translating the entire world container horizontally (all layers equally, no parallax) by the desired distance over 1.5-3s with power2.inOut. In a 3D perspective container, rotate the camera wrapper on Y by 5-20 degrees instead so edges skew subtly. Hold 0.5s before and after the move.

options.what: The camera rotates vertically on the spot, looking up or down.
options.looks: The view slides vertically, revealing above or below; tall subjects revealed top-to-bottom.
options.motion: Smooth vertical sweeps with ease-in-out, often a reveal of height or scale.
options.use: Revealing tall UI (long pages, feeds), towers of stacked cards, vertical timelines, product height reveals.
options.conveys: Scale, discovery, grandeur (tilt up) or grounding (tilt down).
options.vs: A crane or pedestal moves the camera vertically (parallax); a tilt rotates it (no parallax). Scrolling UI is content moving, not the camera.
options.prompt: Tilt by translating the world container vertically (all layers equally) over 1.5-3s with power2.inOut, or in a perspective container rotate the camera wrapper on X by 5-15 degrees. Use for reveals of height; start framed on one end and land framed on the other.

options.what: A pan so fast that the image smears into motion blur, often used to cut between scenes.
options.looks: A burst of horizontal streaking lasting a few frames, then the new framing snaps into place.
options.motion: Explosive acceleration and deceleration (expo.inOut) over 250-450ms, peak blur in the middle, often hiding a cut.
options.use: Energetic transitions, social content, fast-paced feature montages, sports and action.
options.vs: A pan is smooth and readable; a whip pan is a transition device. Whip transition (transitions dimension) is the cut built on it.
options.prompt: Whip pan between scenes: translate the world container 1.5-3 frame widths horizontally over 300-400ms with expo.inOut, applying a horizontal blur (feGaussianBlur stdDeviation 'X 0') that peaks at 30-50 in the middle of the move and returns to 0. Swap the scene at peak blur so the cut is hidden. Land exactly on the new framing with no overshoot.

options.what: The camera moves sideways (or alongside a subject) through space, so nearer objects pass faster than farther ones.
options.looks: Lateral movement with clear parallax: foreground sweeps by, background drifts slowly; feels like traveling past.
options.motion: Constant or gently eased lateral travel, frequently following a moving subject.
options.use: Following a process or journey left to right, passing a row of features, 2.5D photo and illustration scenes.
options.vs: A pan rotates on the spot with little parallax; a track physically moves and creates parallax. US and UK usage of 'track' differ; 'truck' unambiguously means lateral.
options.prompt: Track by translating depth layers horizontally with parallax multipliers (foreground 1.5x, subject 1x, midground 0.5x, background 0.15x of the camera travel), or by translating the camera wrapper in x inside a perspective container with layers at different translateZ. Use sine.inOut or linear with a 300ms ease at each end for constant-speed travel.

options.what: The camera physically moves toward or away from the subject, changing perspective as well as size.
options.looks: Near elements grow faster than far ones, foreground passes out of frame, background changes little; space opens up.
options.motion: Smooth, weighted forward or backward travel (power2.inOut or power1.inOut), often slow.
options.use: Entering a scene, approaching a hero product or UI, spatial interfaces, 2.5D and 3D worlds.
options.vs: A zoom magnifies everything uniformly with no parallax; a dolly changes perspective. Push-in and pull-out are directional dollies, usually slow and motivated.
options.prompt: Dolly by moving through depth, not by uniform scale: in a perspective container (perspective 1200-1600px) animate the camera wrapper's translateZ toward the subject (200-600px over 2-4s, power2.inOut) so layers at different z grow at different rates. In flat 2D, scale each depth layer with its own multiplier (foreground 1.6x, subject 1.25x, background 1.05x). Keep transform-origin on the subject.

options.what: A slow, motivated dolly toward the subject to build intensity or focus.
options.looks: The frame tightens on a subject with intent, then locks; you feel it move.
options.motion: A motivated push that lands: 8-20% over 1-2.5 s (at least 4% a second; a slower push is a creep that shimmers thin lines and small type), power2.inOut or expo.inOut, then locked while the subject acts.
options.use: Emphasizing a key statement, moving toward the product's hero action, emotional beats.
options.vs: A dolly can be any speed and direction; a push-in is slow, forward and emotionally motivated. A zoom-in magnifies without parallax; many 2D pieces use a slow scale that is technically a zoom.
options.prompt: Push in on the subject to go somewhere: scale the world wrapper from 1 to 1.1-1.2 (or translateZ 150-300px in a perspective container) over 1-2.5 s with power2.inOut or expo.inOut, transform-origin on the subject, then lock it while the subject acts. Never a slow push across a whole hold or shot (under 4% a second is a creep). For true depth, give foreground layers a 1.3x multiplier on the same tween.

options.what: The camera moves backward away from the subject, revealing context around it.
options.looks: A detail becomes part of a bigger picture: a button becomes a screen, a screen becomes a device, a device becomes a scene.
options.motion: Starts tight, eases back (power2.inOut, 1.5-3s); often the payoff of a sequence.
options.use: Revealing the whole product after details, macro-to-context stories, ending shots.
options.conveys: Context, scale, resolution, the big picture.
options.vs: A zoom-out magnifies down uniformly; a pull-out reveals new foreground and changes parallax. Infinite zoom repeats the pull-out through nested worlds.
options.prompt: Pull out from a detail to context: start the world wrapper at scale 2.5-4 on the detail (transform-origin on the detail) and ease to 1 over 1.5-3s with power2.inOut, bringing surrounding elements into frame as they finish animating in. For parallax, scale foreground layers from a higher value than background layers.

options.what: The camera rises or descends vertically, often combined with a tilt, as on a crane or jib arm.
options.looks: A sweeping rise over a scene or descent into it; horizons shift, foreground drops away or rises into frame.
options.motion: Large, slow, weighted vertical moves with a compensating tilt (power2.inOut, 3-5s).
options.use: Opening establishing moves, grand reveals, event openers, 3D environments.
options.vs: A tilt rotates the camera without moving it; a crane moves it vertically, producing parallax. A pedestal is a pure vertical move without tilt.
options.prompt: Crane by moving the camera vertically through depth: translate depth layers vertically with parallax multipliers (foreground 1.5x, background 0.2x) while rotating the camera wrapper on X by 5-15 degrees to keep the subject centered; in Three.js move camera.position.y while calling lookAt on the subject. Duration 3-5s, power2.inOut.

options.what: A partial circular move around the subject, keeping it roughly centered while the angle changes.
options.looks: The subject turns relative to the viewer, revealing a side; background shifts in the opposite direction.
options.motion: A curved move of 15-90 degrees, smooth ease-in-out, often slow and elegant.
options.use: Product and device reveals, spatial UI, character moments, 3D logos.
options.vs: An orbit circles further, often a full 360 degrees and sometimes continuously; an arc is a partial, motivated move. Rotating the object is object motion; an arc moves the viewer.
options.prompt: Arc around the subject by rotating the camera wrapper on Y by 20-45 degrees inside a perspective container (perspective 1400px, transform-origin at the subject's depth: '50% 50% -Zpx'), while background layers shift opposite to the rotation. In Three.js move the camera along a circular path and lookAt the subject. 2-3s, power2.inOut.

options.what: The camera circles the subject, often a full revolution or continuously, keeping it centered.
options.looks: The subject is seen from all sides against a rotating background; in product work, a turntable feel.
options.motion: Continuous or long circular motion at constant speed (linear for loops, sine.inOut for single passes).
options.use: Product hero turntables, 3D logos and objects, spatial UI showcases, ambient loops.
options.vs: An arc is partial; an orbit goes most or all of the way round. Rotating the object on a turntable looks similar, but the background and lighting stay fixed; in an orbit they shift.
options.prompt: Orbit only with real 3D (Three.js camera on a circular path at constant radius, lookAt the subject) or pre-rendered footage; for CSS 3D, rotate the scene wrapper on Y 360 degrees with the camera fixed, with backgrounds on a large cylinder or plane that counter-rotates. Loop at constant angular speed (linear, 8-16s per revolution) or single passes of 90-180 degrees with sine.inOut.

options.what: A change of focal length that magnifies or reduces the whole image uniformly without moving the camera.
options.looks: Everything grows or shrinks together with no change in perspective or parallax; flat, graphic, slightly artificial.
options.motion: Scale change of the entire frame; fast crash zooms (200-300ms) or slow creeping zooms.
options.use: UI zooms into detail, map animation, crash-zoom emphasis on social, comedic or documentary emphasis.
options.conveys: Emphasis, scrutiny, urgency (crash zoom) or observation (slow zoom).
options.vs: A dolly moves the camera and changes perspective; a zoom only magnifies. In 2D, uniformly scaling the whole world container is exactly a zoom.
options.prompt: Zoom by uniformly scaling the whole world container with transform-origin set to the point of interest (not the center unless it is the point of interest). Crash zoom: scale 1 to 1.6-2.5 in 200-300ms with expo.out, optionally with a 2-3 frame radial (zoom) blur at peak speed. Slow zoom: 1 to 1.1 over 3-5s linear. No parallax; all layers scale identically.

options.what: Focus shifts from one plane to another within a shot, redirecting attention without moving the camera.
options.looks: A sharp foreground element softens as a blurred background element sharpens (or vice versa).
options.motion: Blur values cross-fade between planes over 400-900ms, ease-in-out; camera stays still.
options.use: Shifting attention between UI and context, foreground label to background product, cinematic 2.5D and spatial scenes.
options.conveys: Attention shift, cinematic intent, storytelling subtlety.
options.vs: Depth-of-field shift is the broader change in focus depth (aperture); rack focus specifically moves the focal plane between two subjects. Depth of field (effects) is the static state.
options.prompt: Rack focus between two depth layers: at the start layer A is blur(0) and layer B blur(8-12px); over 500-800ms with power2.inOut, tween A to blur(8-12px) and B to blur(0). Layers in between reach intermediate blur. Camera and layout stay still during the pull. Only text on the in-focus plane may be read.

options.what: The depth of the in-focus zone widens or narrows, as when a lens aperture opens or closes.
options.looks: A scene goes from shallow focus (only the subject sharp, background dissolved) to deep focus (everything sharp) or the reverse.
options.motion: Background and foreground blur ramps up or down together while the subject stays sharp (600-1200ms).
options.use: Isolating a product or UI element from its context, then returning to context; dreamy reveals.
options.conveys: Isolation, focus, shift from detail to context.
options.vs: Rack focus moves the focal plane between subjects; a DOF shift keeps the subject and changes how much else is sharp.
options.prompt: Shift depth of field around a fixed subject: tween all non-subject layers from blur(0) to blur(6-14px) (proportional to their distance from the subject) over 700-1000ms with power2.inOut to isolate it, optionally dimming them 10-20%; reverse to return to context. The subject layer never blurs.

options.what: The camera looks straight down onto a surface, flattening the scene into a map-like plan.
options.looks: Objects seen from above, like a desk flat lay or a map; shadows fall around objects; no horizon.
options.motion: Objects slide on and off the surface; camera trucks across the plane; rotation around the vertical axis.
options.use: Maps, desk or workspace scenes, board-game-like explainers, product flat lays, food.
options.vs: Isometric views from an elevated diagonal with three visible faces; top-down shows only tops. Orthographic can be any direction; top-down is specifically overhead.
options.prompt: Frame the scene straight overhead: objects show only their top faces, arranged on a flat surface with soft shadows falling evenly around them (top light). Camera moves are trucks across the plane and rotations around the viewing axis (5-15 degrees). Objects slide in from the frame edges as if placed by hand.

options.what: A camera projection with no perspective: parallel lines stay parallel and objects do not shrink with distance.
options.looks: Diagrammatic, model-like views; front, side or angled views without foreshortening.
options.motion: Camera moves change framing and angle but never perspective; zooms are uniform scale.
options.use: Technical and architectural explainers, exploded product views, diagrams, clean 3D icons.
options.vs: Isometric is one specific orthographic angle with equal axes. Perspective camera adds vanishing points. Orthographic 3D (depth dimension) is the construction; this is the camera choice.
options.prompt: Use an orthographic camera: no perspective on any element (no CSS perspective; Three.js OrthographicCamera), parallel edges stay parallel, and distant objects keep their size. Camera moves are trucks, uniform scale zooms and angle changes; never dollies.

options.what: An orthographic camera angled so the three axes appear equally foreshortened at 120 degrees.
options.looks: Diamond-grid view from an elevated corner; three faces of each block visible; no vanishing points.
options.motion: Camera trucks along iso axes, rotates in 90-degree steps, zooms uniformly; the angle stays fixed.
options.use: SaaS and infrastructure explainers, city and system overviews, game-like scenes.
options.conveys: Overview, systematic order, playful model world.
options.vs: Isometric depth (depth dimension) is the drawn world; the isometric camera is the fixed viewing angle. Top-down sees only tops.
options.prompt: Hold an isometric view (orthographic, azimuth 45 degrees, elevation about 35.26 degrees; in CSS rotateX(60deg) rotateZ(-45deg) on the world plane). Move only by trucking along the iso axes and uniform zooms; if the view rotates, rotate in exact 90-degree steps (600-900ms, power2.inOut) so the grid realigns.

options.what: Framing that shows the whole scene or system with the subject small within its context.
options.looks: Many elements visible at once, generous surroundings, the subject placed in relation to everything else.
options.motion: Slow drifts or held frames; often the start (establishing) or end (resolution) of a sequence.
options.use: Establishing a product ecosystem, showing all features or devices together, ending pull-outs.
options.vs: A wide-angle lens (short focal length) exaggerates perspective; a wide shot is framing and can be made with any lens. Extreme close-up is the opposite framing.
options.prompt: Frame wide: the whole scene or system visible with the subject occupying 15-30% of frame and at least 10% margin around the outermost elements. Hold or drift slowly (scale 1 to 1.03 over the shot). Use a wide shot to establish before cutting or pushing into detail.

options.what: Extreme magnification of a small detail, with very shallow depth of field, as a macro lens records.
options.looks: A tiny detail (a UI toggle, a texture, a product edge) fills the frame; background dissolves into blur; surface detail becomes graphic.
options.motion: Slow slides across the detail, gentle focus shifts, micro-movements feel large.
options.use: Product craftsmanship shots, UI micro-interactions shown huge, texture and material reveals.
options.vs: Extreme close-up is a framing on part of a subject; macro implies optical magnification with very shallow focus. Oversized UI (UI treatment) enlarges a component as a design choice, not a lens.
options.prompt: Shoot a macro: scale the world container 4-10x onto the detail (transform-origin on it), blur everything outside a narrow focal band (filter blur 6-12px on non-focal layers, or a radial mask-blur), and move slowly (translate 3-8% of frame over 2-4s, sine.inOut). Ensure the magnified asset is high-resolution vector or 3x+ raster.

options.what: Framing so tight that only part of the subject fills the frame: a word, a button, a corner of a device.
options.looks: Cropped, bold, abstract; the subject exceeds the frame on at least one side.
options.motion: Quick cuts between ECUs, short slides across the subject, punch-ins on beats.
options.use: Kinetic typography, feature montages, product detail cuts, dramatic emphasis.
options.vs: Macro implies magnification with shallow focus; an ECU is simply a very tight crop and can be crisp throughout. A wide shot is the opposite.
options.prompt: Frame extreme close-ups: crop so the subject overflows the frame on at least two sides (scale 3-6x with transform-origin on the detail) and only one element is readable. Cut between ECUs on beats or punch in with 150-250ms expo.out scale steps. Keep assets vector or high-resolution.

options.what: A camera move faked in 2D by moving depth layers at different speeds, producing depth from motion.
options.looks: A flat illustration or photo gains depth as the camera drifts: foreground slides faster than background.
options.motion: Slow drifts, trucks and push-ins across layered artwork; all layers share one ease.
options.use: Photo animation, illustrated brand films, landing-page heroes, documentary graphics.
options.conveys: Depth, immersion, cinematic life in still artwork.
options.vs: A track in real 3D produces parallax naturally; a parallax camera fakes it with speed multipliers. Parallax (depth dimension) is the layered construction; this is the move.
options.prompt: Fake the camera with parallax multipliers: split the scene into 3-5 layers and on one shared tween move them by camera_travel times a multiplier (foreground 1.6x, subject 1x, midground 0.5x, background 0.15x); for push-ins scale layers with multipliers (1.25x, 1.1x, 1.04x, 1.01x). Oversize edge layers 10-15% so no edge enters frame. Use sine.inOut over 3-6s.

options.what: Small, irregular, organic drift and rotation of the frame imitating a camera held by hand.
options.looks: The frame breathes: slight wandering translation and rotation; graphics feel documented rather than designed.
options.motion: Low-frequency wander (a few pixels, under 1 degree of rotation), with occasional sharper bumps on impacts.
options.use: Documentary-style graphics, graphics composited into handheld footage, urgent or intimate moments, social content.
options.vs: Camera shake on impact is a brief jolt; handheld simulation is continuous gentle wander. A locked camera has none.
options.prompt: Simulate handheld by driving the world container with smooth pseudo-noise computed from timeline time: x and y = sum of 2-3 sines at incommensurate frequencies (0.3-1.2 Hz) with 3-8px total amplitude, rotation up to 0.4 degrees, and scale fixed at 1.03 to hide edges. Add a 3-6px jolt decaying over 250ms on impacts. Never use unseeded randomness.

options.what: The whole piece (or a long sequence) plays as one unbroken camera move traveling across a large world from scene to scene.
options.looks: No cuts: scenes are laid out across a big canvas or 3D space; each new idea arrives as the camera glides, pans, dives or rises to it.
options.motion: Linked moves with overlapping eases (each move begins before the last settles), holds at each station, varied directions to avoid monotony.
options.use: SaaS launch films, feature tours, infinite-canvas explainers, brand journeys, landing-page heroes.
options.conveys: Flow, coherence, connectedness; everything is part of one system.
options.vs: Cuts and transitions replace the frame; a continuous journey only moves through one persistent world. Infinite zoom is a continuous journey along the depth axis only.
options.prompt: Lay out every scene as a station on one large world canvas (e.g. 6000x4000px or a 3D space) and play the piece as a single camera path: move the world container between stations with power3.inOut over 900-1500ms, holding 2-4s per station while local elements animate. Vary direction (right, down, into depth) and start each move 150-250ms before the previous scene's last element settles. No cuts.

options.what: A continuous zoom into (or out of) nested worlds, where each detail contains the next scene, seemingly forever.
options.looks: A detail grows to become a whole scene, within which another detail grows to become the next scene; seamless loop possible.
options.motion: Exponential scale (constant perceived speed), each level handing off to the next with matching composition; often ends where it began.
options.use: Micro-to-macro narratives, loops, music videos, feature journeys ('inside the product'), brand manifestos.
options.vs: A zoom is one magnification; infinite zoom chains nested levels. Zoom-through transition passes through one element once.
options.prompt: Nest 3-6 scenes so each lives inside a detail of the previous one at a fixed ratio (e.g. level n+1 is 1/8 the size of level n, positioned in its focal detail). Zoom by tweening a single progress value and deriving scale as ratio^progress (exponential, so speed feels constant), with transform-origin locked on the nested detail; use ease 'none' through the chain and power2 only at the start and end. Fade in each inner level as it passes 20-30% of frame width, and remove outer levels once off-screen.
